questions.question: The SI unit of force is
questions.answer: newton
questions.explanation: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s² — the SI unit of force.

questions.question: The property of a body by virtue of which it resists changes in its state of motion is called
questions.answer: inertia
questions.explanation: Inertia is the resistance to a change in motion. Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia.

questions.question: Which of the following best illustrates inertia of motion?
options: A ball at rest on a table
A passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly
A book on a slowly moving conveyor belt
Dust falling off a carpet when beaten
questions.answer: A passenger lurches forward when a bus stops suddenly
questions.explanation: The passenger's body, by inertia of motion, tends to continue moving forward even after the bus has decelerated.

questions.question: Newton's first law of motion is also known as the
questions.answer: law of inertia
questions.explanation: The first law asserts that a body retains its state (rest or uniform motion) unless an external force acts on it — i.e. inertia.

questions.question: Newton's first law is valid in
questions.answer: only inertial frames
questions.explanation: Newton's laws hold in inertial (non-accelerating) frames. In non-inertial frames, pseudo-forces must be introduced.

questions.question: A force of 20 N is applied to a body of mass 4 kg. The acceleration of the body is
questions.answer: 5 m/s²

questions.question: A 2-kg body accelerates at 3 m/s². The net force on it is
questions.answer: 6 N

questions.question: A ball of mass 0.2 kg moving at 5 m/s is brought to rest in 0.5 s. The average force needed is
questions.answer: 2 N

questions.question: The momentum of a 5-kg body moving at 4 m/s is
questions.answer: 20 kg·m/s

questions.question: The impulse on a body equals
questions.answer: force × time = change in momentum
questions.explanation: Impulse J = F Δt = Δp by Newton's second law in integrated form.

questions.question: Newton's third law states that
options: every body continues in its state of rest or motion
every action has an equal and opposite reaction
questions.answer: every action has an equal and opposite reaction
questions.explanation: Third law: when body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A.

questions.question: Action-reaction force pairs
options: always cancel each other and produce no motion
act on the same body and cancel
act on different bodies and therefore do not cancel
questions.answer: act on different bodies and therefore do not cancel
questions.explanation: Action-reaction forces always act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they don't cancel each other in any free-body diagram of a single body.

questions.question: A bullet of mass 0.01 kg is fired from a 5-kg gun with velocity 200 m/s. The recoil velocity of the gun is
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: m₁v₁ = m₂v₂ ⇒ 0.01 × 200 = 5 × v ⇒ v = 0.4 m/s (in the opposite direction).

questions.question: Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 3 kg moving with velocities 4 m/s and 2 m/s respectively in the same direction collide and stick together. Their common velocity after collision is
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: 2×4 + 3×2 = (2+3) × v ⇒ 14 = 5v ⇒ v = 2.8 m/s.

questions.question: Conservation of linear momentum holds when
options: no external force acts on the system
the bodies in the system are identical
questions.answer: no external force acts on the system
questions.explanation: The total external force determines the rate of change of total momentum. Zero external force ⇒ constant total momentum.

questions.question: The maximum static friction force is given by
questions.answer: μ_s N
questions.explanation: f_s,max = μ_s N where N is the normal force. Below this value, f_s adjusts to balance the applied force.

questions.question: Kinetic friction is given by
questions.answer: μ_k N
questions.explanation: f_k = μ_k N, where μ_k < μ_s for most surfaces.

questions.question: Which of the following is generally TRUE for friction?
questions.answer: μ_s > μ_k
questions.explanation: It usually takes more force to start an object sliding than to keep it sliding; hence μ_s > μ_k.

questions.question: A 10-kg block sits on a rough floor with μ_s = 0.4. The minimum horizontal force to just start moving it is (g = 10 m/s²)
A 5-kg block slides on a rough floor with μ_k = 0.2. The friction force on it is (g = 10 m/s²)
A 2-kg block slides down a smooth incline at 30°. Its acceleration is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: 5 m/s²
questions.explanation: a = g sin θ = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s² (only the gravity component along the slope; normal force balances perpendicular component).

questions.question: On a smooth incline at angle θ, the normal force on a block of mass m is
questions.answer: mg cos θ
questions.explanation: Perpendicular equilibrium: N = mg cos θ. (Parallel direction is where the net force ma comes from.)

questions.question: Two masses m₁ = 3 kg and m₂ = 2 kg are connected over a frictionless pulley (Atwood machine). The acceleration of the system is (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: 2 m/s²

questions.question: If the net external force on a body is zero, the body
options: moves with constant velocity (which may be zero)
questions.answer: moves with constant velocity (which may be zero)
questions.explanation: Newton's first law: zero net force ⇒ constant velocity (rest is the special case v = 0).

questions.question: A 1-kg ball strikes a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 8 m/s in the opposite direction. The magnitude of the change in momentum is
questions.answer: 18 kg·m/s
questions.explanation: Δp = m(v − u) = 1 × (−8 − 10) = −18 kg·m/s; magnitude = 18 kg·m/s. (Signs matter — the velocity reverses direction.)

questions.question: A rocket gains forward momentum by ejecting exhaust gases. This is an example of
options: Conservation of momentum / Newton's third law
questions.answer: Conservation of momentum / Newton's third law
questions.explanation: The rocket pushes the gases backward; by Newton's third law, gases push the rocket forward. Total momentum of (rocket + gases) is conserved.

questions.question: A horse pulls a cart. The horse moves the cart forward because
options: the horse pulls the cart with more force than the cart pulls the horse
the cart pulls the horse with less force than the horse pulls the cart
the horse pushes backward on the ground; the ground pushes forward on the horse
action and reaction cancel out everything
questions.answer: the horse pushes backward on the ground; the ground pushes forward on the horse
questions.explanation: The horse's hooves push backward on the ground; by Newton's third law, the ground pushes the horse (and so the system) forward. The horse–cart action–reaction pair acts on different bodies and does not cancel within either single body.

questions.question: Two blocks of masses 5 kg and 3 kg are connected by a string and pulled by a horizontal force of 40 N applied to the 5-kg block on a smooth horizontal surface. The acceleration of the system is
questions.answer: 5 m/s²
questions.explanation: Total mass = 8 kg. a = F / (m₁ + m₂) = 40 / 8 = 5 m/s².

questions.question: A body in motion at constant velocity has zero net force on it.
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: By Newton's first law, constant velocity (which includes rest) requires zero net external force.

questions.question: Action-reaction forces, being equal and opposite, always cancel out and produce no motion.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: They act on DIFFERENT bodies, so they do not cancel within a free-body diagram of either single body. Each body may have non-zero net force from the OTHER forces in its own diagram.

questions.question: If two bodies collide on a frictionless table, the total momentum just after the collision is the same as just before.
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: On a frictionless table no external horizontal force acts, so the total horizontal momentum is conserved.

questions.question: The maximum static friction depends on the area of contact between the surfaces.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: To a good approximation, f_s,max = μ_s N depends only on the normal force, NOT on the apparent area of contact (because the real microscopic contact area is what matters and that scales with N).

questions.question: Newton's second law in vector form is F = ____.
questions.answer: m a
questions.explanation: F = ma, or more generally F = dp/dt.

questions.question: The momentum of a body of mass m moving at velocity v is p = ____.
questions.answer: m v
questions.explanation: Linear momentum: p = mv, a vector along v.

questions.question: Impulse = ____ × time = change in ____.
questions.answer: force; momentum
questions.explanation: Impulse J = F Δt = Δp.

questions.question: Kinetic friction force on a sliding body is f_k = ____.
questions.answer: μ_k N
questions.explanation: Where μ_k is the coefficient of kinetic friction and N is the normal force.

questions.question: On a smooth incline of angle θ, a block of mass m experiences a gravitational component along the slope equal to ____.
questions.answer: m g sin θ
questions.explanation: The component of gravity along the incline is mg sin θ; perpendicular is mg cos θ.

questions.question: Define inertia. Name the three kinds of inertia and give one example of each.
questions.answer: Inertia is the property of a body by virtue of which it resists any change in its state of motion. (i) Inertia of rest — a book on a table stays at rest until someone pushes it. (ii) Inertia of motion — a passenger continues to move forward when a bus stops suddenly. (iii) Inertia of direction — mud flying off the tyre of a vehicle continues in a straight line tangentially.

questions.question: State Newton's first law of motion. Why is it called the law of inertia?
questions.answer: Newton's first law: a body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external force. It is called the law of inertia because it codifies the property of inertia: a body's natural tendency is to keep doing what it is doing (resting or moving uniformly), and a force is needed to change that.

questions.question: A 5-kg ball is accelerated from rest to 10 m/s in 2 s. Find the magnitude of the average force.
questions.answer: Acceleration: a = (v − u)/t = (10 − 0)/2 = 5 m/s². Force: F = ma = 5 × 5 = 25 N. (Or use Δp/Δt directly: Δp = 50 kg·m/s, Δt = 2 s, F = 25 N.)

questions.question: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 30 m/s is caught by a fielder in 0.05 s. Find the average force on the ball and explain (in one sentence) why fielders pull their hands back while catching.
questions.answer: Δp = m Δv = 0.15 × (0 − 30) = −4.5 kg·m/s. |F| = |Δp| / Δt = 4.5 / 0.05 = 90 N. Fielders pull their hands back to INCREASE Δt — for the same Δp, a larger Δt means a smaller force (and less risk of injury).

questions.question: State Newton's third law. Why do the action and reaction forces not cancel each other?
questions.answer: Newton's third law: whenever a body A exerts a force on body B, body B exerts an equal and opposite force on body A. The two forces do not cancel because they act on DIFFERENT bodies; in the free-body diagram of either body, only ONE of the pair appears.

questions.question: A 5-g bullet is fired from a 2-kg rifle with a velocity of 400 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the rifle.
questions.answer: Conservation of momentum (system at rest before firing): m₁ v₁ + m₂ v₂ = 0, where m₁ = 0.005 kg (bullet) at v₁ = 400 m/s and m₂ = 2 kg (rifle) at recoil v₂. Solving: v₂ = −(0.005 × 400) / 2 = −1 m/s. The rifle recoils at 1 m/s in the direction opposite to the bullet.

questions.question: A 60-kg ice skater pushes off another 40-kg skater initially at rest. The 40-kg skater moves at 3 m/s afterward. Find the recoil velocity of the 60-kg skater.
questions.answer: Initial momentum = 0 (both at rest). Final: 60 × v_60 + 40 × 3 = 0 ⇒ 60 v_60 = −120 ⇒ v_60 = −2 m/s. The 60-kg skater recoils at 2 m/s in the opposite direction.

questions.question: Explain how Newton's third law leads to conservation of linear momentum for an isolated system of two bodies.
questions.answer: Consider two bodies A and B with no external force. By Newton's third law, F_AB = −F_BA (force A exerts on B equals minus force B exerts on A). By Newton's second law: dp_A/dt = F_BA and dp_B/dt = F_AB. Adding: d(p_A + p_B)/dt = F_AB + F_BA = 0. So p_A + p_B = constant — total momentum is conserved.

questions.question: A 10-kg block lies on a horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 50 N is just sufficient to start the block sliding, after which a 30-N force keeps it moving at constant velocity. Find μ_s and μ_k. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: Normal force N = mg = 100 N. μ_s = F_min,start / N = 50 / 100 = 0.5. μ_k = F_constant / N = 30 / 100 = 0.3. As expected, μ_s > μ_k.

questions.question: A 4-kg block is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of 25 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Find the acceleration of the block. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: Friction force: f_k = μ_k m g = 0.3 × 4 × 10 = 12 N. Net force: F_net = 25 − 12 = 13 N. Acceleration: a = F_net / m = 13 / 4 = 3.25 m/s².

questions.question: A 2-kg block slides down a smooth (frictionless) incline that makes 30° with the horizontal. Find (i) its acceleration, (ii) the normal force on it. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer:
(i) Along the slope: net force = m g sin θ ⇒ a = g sin θ = 10 × 0.5 = 5 m/s² down the slope.
(ii) Perpendicular to slope: equilibrium ⇒ N = m g cos θ = 2 × 10 × (√3/2) = 10√3 ≈ 17.3 N.

questions.question: Two blocks of masses 4 kg and 6 kg are tied by a string passing over a smooth massless pulley. Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string. (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.answer: Atwood-machine analysis. Take the heavier block (6 kg) descending. For 6 kg: 6g − T = 6a. For 4 kg: T − 4g = 4a. Add: 2g = 10a ⇒ a = 2 m/s². From 4 kg eqn: T = 4(g + a) = 4 × 12 = 48 N.

questions.question: A force-time graph for a ball shows a constant force of 4 N applied for 0.5 s. Find the impulse delivered, and (if the ball had mass 0.2 kg and was initially at rest) its final velocity.
questions.answer: Impulse = F × Δt = 4 × 0.5 = 2 N·s. Final velocity from impulse-momentum theorem: m v = J ⇒ v = 2 / 0.2 = 10 m/s.

questions.question: When you jump off a small boat onto a jetty, the boat moves backward. Use Newton's third law and momentum conservation to explain.
questions.answer: When you push backward on the boat with your legs to launch yourself forward, the boat pushes you forward by Newton's third law — and you push backward on it. Treating you+boat as an isolated system (water friction ignored briefly), total momentum is initially zero; after the jump you carry forward momentum p₁ = m_you × v_you, so the boat carries backward momentum p₂ = −p₁ to keep the total zero. The boat recoils at v_boat = −(m_you / m_boat) × v_you.

questions.question: Two bodies of masses 2 kg and 3 kg moving toward each other with velocities 4 m/s and 1 m/s (respectively) collide and stick together. Find the velocity of the combined mass after collision.
questions.answer: Take direction of the 2-kg body as positive. p_before = 2(+4) + 3(−1) = 8 − 3 = 5 kg·m/s. After: (2+3) v = 5 ⇒ v = 1 m/s in the direction of the 2-kg body (positive).

questions.question: State and explain Newton's second law of motion. Show that F = ma is a special case of F = dp/dt.
questions.answer:
Newton's second law: the rate of change of linear momentum of a body is directly proportional to the net external force applied on it, and the change in momentum takes place in the direction of the applied force. In SI units, F = dp/dt.

Momentum p = mv. If mass is constant (the usual case in mechanics):
  F = dp/dt = d(mv)/dt = m dv/dt = m a.

So F = ma is the constant-mass special case of the more general F = dp/dt. The general form is needed for systems where mass varies — e.g. rockets ejecting fuel, raindrops gaining mass, or conveyor belts being loaded with sand.

questions.question: State the principle of conservation of linear momentum. Derive it using Newton's second and third laws for an isolated two-body system. Give one practical application.
questions.answer:
Principle: in the absence of external forces, the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant.

Derivation for two bodies A and B with no external force, only mutual interaction force:
 - Force on A due to B: F_BA. By Newton's second law: dp_A/dt = F_BA.
 - Force on B due to A: F_AB. By Newton's second law: dp_B/dt = F_AB.
 - By Newton's third law: F_AB = −F_BA.
 - Adding: d(p_A + p_B)/dt = F_BA + F_AB = 0.
 - So p_A + p_B = constant.

Application: rocket propulsion. The rocket ejects exhaust gases backward; the system (rocket + exhausted gas) has constant total momentum, so the rocket gains forward momentum equal in magnitude to the backward momentum of the gases.

questions.question: A 3-kg block is placed on a rough horizontal floor (μ_s = 0.5, μ_k = 0.3). A horizontal force F is applied to the block. Discuss what happens (a) when F = 10 N, (b) when F = 14 N, (c) when F = 20 N. Take g = 10 m/s².
questions.answer:
Normal force N = mg = 30 N. Maximum static friction f_s,max = μ_s N = 15 N. Kinetic friction (once moving) f_k = μ_k N = 9 N.

(a) F = 10 N < 15 N: the block stays at rest. Static friction adjusts to exactly cancel F, so f_s = 10 N. Net force = 0, acceleration = 0.

(b) F = 14 N < 15 N: still below threshold. Block remains at rest; static friction = 14 N. The block has NOT YET started moving.

(c) F = 20 N > 15 N: the applied force exceeds maximum static friction; the block starts sliding. Once moving, kinetic friction takes over (f_k = 9 N). Net force = 20 − 9 = 11 N. Acceleration = 11 / 3 ≈ 3.67 m/s².

questions.question: A block of mass m on a rough incline of angle θ. State (i) the condition for the block to be on the verge of sliding down, (ii) the condition for it to slide down at constant velocity, (iii) the condition for it to remain at rest no matter how rough the surface. Use μ_s and μ_k as needed.
questions.answer:
Forces along the slope: gravity component down the slope is mg sin θ; friction acts up the slope and adjusts up to μ_s mg cos θ (static) or equals μ_k mg cos θ (kinetic).

(i) Verge of sliding down: the maximum static friction just balances gravity along the slope: mg sin θ = μ_s mg cos θ ⇒ tan θ = μ_s. The angle θ_c = arctan(μ_s) is called the angle of repose.

(ii) Sliding down at constant velocity (zero acceleration): kinetic friction exactly balances gravity along the slope: mg sin θ = μ_k mg cos θ ⇒ tan θ = μ_k.

(iii) For the block to remain at rest no matter how rough, we'd need static friction to balance the gravitational pull even for θ = 90°, which means μ_s = ∞ — impossible. For any finite μ_s, there is always a θ above which the block slides (the angle of repose).

questions.question: Two everyday phenomena that look like exceptions to Newton's third law: (a) a person walks forward by pushing the ground backward; (b) a magnet attracts a piece of iron from a distance. Explain how the third law actually applies in each.
questions.answer:
(a) Walking forward: the foot pushes the ground BACKWARD with force F. By Newton's third law, the ground pushes the foot (and person) FORWARD with force F. Friction is what allows the foot to grip the ground and transmit this push — on a frictionless surface (ice) the foot just slides without producing forward motion.

(b) Magnet and iron: the magnet exerts an attractive force on the iron toward itself; by Newton's third law the iron exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet (attracting it toward the iron). Both bodies experience equal-magnitude attractive forces; if both are free to move, both accelerate toward each other (with the lighter one accelerating more).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A 1500-kg car is moving at 20 m/s when its brakes are applied. The car decelerates uniformly and comes to rest in 5 seconds.

(i) Find the deceleration.
(ii) Find the magnitude of the braking force.
(iii) Find the distance covered during braking.
(iv) If a 1500-kg truck travels at the same speed and is braked by the same force, how far does it travel before stopping?
questions.answer:
(i) v = u + at ⇒ 0 = 20 + a × 5 ⇒ a = −4 m/s². Deceleration = 4 m/s².
(ii) F = m|a| = 1500 × 4 = 6000 N.
(iii) s = u t + (1/2) a t² = 20 × 5 − (1/2) × 4 × 25 = 100 − 50 = 50 m.
(iv) Same mass and same force, so same deceleration ⇒ same stopping distance = 50 m. (The wording said 'truck' but with the same mass and force the answer is identical — a useful demonstration that stopping distance depends on u, m and F.)

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A 2-kg ball is held above a 1-kg book resting on the floor. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) Identify the action-reaction pair between Earth and the ball.
(ii) Identify the action-reaction pair between the book and the floor.
(iii) The Earth attracts the book with a force of 10 N (weight). What force does the book exert on the Earth, and in what direction?
(iv) Why do the two forces in (iii) not cancel each other in the free-body diagram of the book?
questions.answer:
(i) Earth pulls the ball down (gravity, magnitude mg = 20 N). Ball pulls Earth up with an equal 20 N gravitational force. These are the action-reaction pair.
(ii) The book pushes the floor down with the contact force; the floor pushes the book up by the same force (normal reaction). These are the action-reaction contact pair.
(iii) By Newton's third law, the book attracts the Earth with 10 N upward (toward the book). Direction is opposite to Earth's attraction on the book.
(iv) Action-reaction forces act on DIFFERENT bodies — Earth's pull on the book acts on the book; the book's pull on Earth acts on Earth. In the free-body diagram of the book ONLY the forces on the book appear (gravity from Earth + normal from floor), and these two DO balance each other to keep the book at rest. The book's pull on Earth doesn't appear in the book's diagram at all.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A 50-g bullet is fired horizontally with a velocity of 600 m/s into a 5-kg wooden block placed on a smooth horizontal surface. The bullet gets embedded in the block.

(i) Use conservation of momentum to find the velocity of the (block + bullet) system immediately after impact.
(ii) Find the kinetic energy of the bullet just before impact.
(iii) Find the kinetic energy of the (block + bullet) just after impact.
(iv) Is energy conserved in this collision? Where does the difference go?
questions.answer:
(i) Initial p = 0.050 × 600 + 5 × 0 = 30 kg·m/s. Final p = (5 + 0.050) × v ⇒ v = 30 / 5.050 ≈ 5.94 m/s.
(ii) KE_before = (1/2) × 0.050 × 600² = (1/2) × 0.050 × 360000 = 9000 J.
(iii) KE_after = (1/2) × 5.050 × 5.94² ≈ (1/2) × 5.050 × 35.3 ≈ 89.1 J.
(iv) Energy is NOT conserved (this is an inelastic collision). About 9000 − 89 = 8911 J is dissipated as heat, sound, deformation of the wood and the bullet, etc. Momentum IS conserved (no external horizontal force); energy is generally not in inelastic collisions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A 20-kg block sits on a horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction is 0.4 and the coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) What is the maximum static friction the floor can supply?
(ii) A horizontal force of 60 N is applied. Does the block move? If so, what is its acceleration?
(iii) A horizontal force of 100 N is applied. What is the block's acceleration?
(iv) Once the block is moving, what happens to the friction force? Explain.
questions.answer:
(i) f_s,max = μ_s m g = 0.4 × 20 × 10 = 80 N.
(ii) 60 N < 80 N — block stays at rest. Static friction = 60 N (adjusts to balance). a = 0.
(iii) 100 N > 80 N — block moves. Friction becomes kinetic: f_k = μ_k m g = 0.25 × 200 = 50 N. Net force = 100 − 50 = 50 N. a = 50 / 20 = 2.5 m/s².
(iv) Once sliding, kinetic friction (smaller, fixed at μ_k N) takes over from static friction (which could go up to μ_s N). This sudden drop is why it often takes a hard push to start something moving, but then it suddenly accelerates.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A block of mass 4 kg slides down a smooth incline that makes an angle of 37° with the horizontal. The incline is 5 m long. Take sin 37° = 0.6, cos 37° = 0.8, g = 10 m/s².

(i) Find the acceleration of the block down the incline.
(ii) Find the normal force on the block from the incline.
(iii) Find the speed of the block at the bottom of the incline, given it started from rest at the top.
(iv) How long does the block take to reach the bottom?

Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

A 5-kg block (m₁) on a smooth horizontal table is connected by a light string passing over a frictionless pulley to a 3-kg block (m₂) hanging vertically. The system is released from rest. Take g = 10 m/s².

(i) Identify the forces acting on each block.
(ii) Find the acceleration of the system.
(iii) Find the tension in the string.
(iv) How far does each block move in the first 2 seconds?
questions.answer:
(i) On m₁: weight (down), normal (up), tension T (horizontal, toward pulley). On m₂: weight m₂ g (down), tension T (up).
(ii) For m₁: T = m₁ a. For m₂: m₂ g − T = m₂ a. Add: m₂ g = (m₁ + m₂) a ⇒ a = m₂ g / (m₁ + m₂) = 30 / 8 = 3.75 m/s².
(iii) T = m₁ a = 5 × 3.75 = 18.75 N.
(iv) Both blocks have the same acceleration (linked by inextensible string). s = (1/2) a t² = (1/2) × 3.75 × 4 = 7.5 m each.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

Two trolleys of masses 2 kg and 4 kg sit on a frictionless track. They are pushed apart by a compressed spring placed between them. After release, the 2-kg trolley moves to the left at 6 m/s.

(i) State the principle being used.
(ii) What is the velocity of the 4-kg trolley after release?
(iii) Find the total kinetic energy of the system after release.
(iv) Where did this kinetic energy come from?
questions.answer:
(i) Conservation of linear momentum — no external horizontal force on the (trolley + trolley + spring) system.
(ii) p_before = 0. After: 2(−6) + 4(v) = 0 ⇒ v = 3 m/s to the right.
(iii) KE = (1/2)(2)(6²) + (1/2)(4)(3²) = 36 + 18 = 54 J.
(iv) From the elastic potential energy stored in the compressed spring before release. The spring transferred its stored PE to the KE of the two trolleys.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.

In an explosion, a stationary firecracker of mass 0.6 kg breaks into three fragments. Two fragments of equal mass 0.2 kg each move horizontally in mutually perpendicular directions at 4 m/s each.

(i) State the principle of conservation of momentum and explain why it applies here.
(ii) Find the resultant momentum of the two equal fragments.
(iii) Find the momentum of the third fragment (in magnitude and direction).
(iv) Find the velocity of the third fragment.
questions.answer:
(i) Total momentum of an isolated system is conserved. The explosion involves only internal forces (no significant external impulse during the very short explosion time), so total momentum of the three pieces equals the initial momentum (zero, since the cracker was at rest).
(ii) Each has momentum 0.2 × 4 = 0.8 kg·m/s in mutually perpendicular directions. Resultant = √(0.8² + 0.8²) = 0.8√2 ≈ 1.13 kg·m/s, at 45° between the two fragments.
(iii) For the total to be zero, the third fragment's momentum must be 0.8√2 kg·m/s in the OPPOSITE direction (at 45° between the two fragments, but pointing the other way).
(iv) Mass of third fragment = 0.6 − 0.2 − 0.2 = 0.2 kg. Velocity = momentum / mass = 0.8√2 / 0.2 = 4√2 ≈ 5.66 m/s, opposite to the bisector of the other two.
